subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical primary amine whose conjugate acid has a pKa of 9.4 is placed in a buffered solution at pH 7.4. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The amine precipitates as a neutral solid because acid removes its hydrogen bonding ability
The nitrogen donates a proton to water, giving an anion that is less water soluble
The amine stays neutral because nitrogen's lone pair is already committed to bonding
The nitrogen lone pair accepts a proton, giving a cation that is more water soluble

explanation:
Amines are weak bases because the nonbonding electron pair on nitrogen can accept a proton, producing a substituted ammonium cation (R—NH3+). By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, the protonated form exceeds the neutral form by 10^(9.4 − 7.4) = 100 to 1 at pH 7.4, so the amine is overwhelmingly ionized. The full positive charge greatly strengthens ion-dipole interaction with water, which is why amine-containing drugs are commonly formulated as hydrochloride salts to improve dissolution.

ELI-10: Nitrogen in an amine has one pair of electrons not used in bonding, and a proton is simply a bare positive charge looking for electrons, so the two combine readily. When the pH sits below the conjugate acid's pKa, the protonated form wins, and here 9.4 − 7.4 = 2 pH units below means it wins by 10^2, or 100 to 1. That single charge is what makes the molecule dissolve well in water, the same reason sodium chloride dissolves and cooking oil does not.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
